skill.name: Monitor: spot the sentence that contradicts the rest
skill.why: Good readers notice when something doesn't add up, then go back and check.
skill.how: Hold the facts in your head. When a sentence clashes with them, stop and check.

steps.say: Good readers keep asking: does this still make sense? Read about Noodle.

show.text: Noodle is a pure white dog.
show.nudge: That's the fact. Does every other sentence agree with it?

show.text: His white fur gets dirty fast.
show.nudge: White fur agrees with a white dog. Keep looking.

show.text: In the sun, his black fur shone.

show.nudge: A white dog can love the beach. That fits.

steps.ask: One sentence can't be true if the others are. Tap it.
steps.win: Yes! Noodle can't be pure white AND have black fur. That's a contradiction.

steps.say: A contradiction means two sentences can't both be true. So what should I do?

show.text: Noodle is a pure white dog.
In the sun, his black fur shone.

steps.ask: What does a good reader do next?

options.text: Go back and re-read the fact.
Ignore it and keep going.
options.reason: If you ignore it, you might get the whole text wrong. Stop and check.

options.text: Skip to the end.
options.reason: The end won't fix it. Go back to where the trouble started.

steps.win: Yes! Go back to the fact and check. Checking as you read is called monitoring.

steps.say: Careful! A surprise isn't always a contradiction. Read this one.

show.text: Noodle is a pure white dog.
Then he rolled in mud and came out brown.

steps.ask: Do these two sentences contradict each other?

check.nudge: Can a white dog get muddy? After a bath, is he white again?

steps.win: Right! Mud doesn't change his real fur. Both can be true, so they don't clash.

steps.say: Some clashes take a bit of thinking. Count carefully.

show.text: Three kids ran the race: Kira, Josh and Mo.
show.nudge: That's the fact to count from. Three runners.
Someone has to win. Josh first fits.
Second fits with three runners. Keep counting.

steps.ask: Tap the sentence that can't be true.
steps.win: Yes! There were only three runners, so nobody can come fourth.

steps.say: Your turn. Find the fact first. Then test every sentence against it.

show.text: Ari has never seen the sea.
show.nudge: That's the fact. Test the other sentences against it.
The desert is far from the sea. That fits.

show.text: Last summer, he swam in the sea.

show.nudge: He hopes to see waves because he never has. That fits.

steps.ask: Tap the sentence that contradicts the rest.
steps.win: Yes! Ari has never seen the sea, so he can't have swum in it.

terms.means: A sentence the rest of the text agrees with. Keep it in your head.
A sentence that can't be true if the fact is true. The two clash.

creature.name: Glowerbill
creature.blurb: A frogmouth that sits as still as a branch, half asleep. When a sentence doesn't add up, its eyes snap wide open.

write.ask: Rewrite the last sentence so it no longer clashes with the facts about Pip.
given: Pip the puppy is scared of water.
She hides under the bed at bath time.
At the beach, Pip raced straight into the waves.
checks: My sentence fits the fact that Pip fears water.
It still says what Pip did at the beach.
write.model: At the beach, Pip sat far up on the dry sand and barked at every wave.

encounters.frame: A space station diary drifted onto Hollowgum Island. The Glowerbill has found a problem.
encounters.text: Day 112 on the space station. Our station circles the whole Earth about every ninety minutes, so we see a sunrise around sixteen times a day. At first, the constant sunrises made it hard to sleep, so we wear eye masks and keep our windows covered at bedtime. Today I did my two hours of exercise on the treadmill, strapped down with bungee cords so I wouldn't float away. My crewmate Raj has grown two centimetres since we arrived, because his spine stretches when gravity isn't pulling it down. He's very proud of this. Then I fixed a leaking water pipe, which was tricky because the water drifted around in wobbly bubbles. In the afternoon, I spoke to a school class back on Earth. One student asked what I miss most, and I said rain. I've only seen one sunrise in all my time up here, so I really miss mornings too. Tonight we're having space tacos, which means wraps, because bread makes crumbs that float into the equipment.
encounters.prompt: Which sentence contradicts the rest of the diary?

options.reason: This fits. Constant sunrises match seeing about sixteen a day.

options.reason: Surprising, but it doesn't clash. The diary explains why: no gravity pulling on his spine.

encounters.frame: Mo is planning food for a camping trip. The Glowerbill is checking his plan.
encounters.text: The crew is going camping for three days at Stringybark Flat. There's no electricity at the campsite, and there's a total fire ban, so nobody can light a campfire or use any kind of stove. Mo has been put in charge of food, which worries everyone. To be fair, he has thought hard about it this time. He has planned meals that don't need cooking: wraps, fruit, nuts, cheese and his famous cold pasta salad. Everything has to fit into two eskies, because the campsite is a long walk from the car park. The walk in takes about forty minutes. Mo has also packed a huge bag of ice to keep the cheese and milk cold. Gus has asked whether he can bring his pet cockroach, and the answer was a firm no. Tully has made a list of jobs, and Zed has already swapped all of his with somebody else. Wren is bringing a first-aid kit and enough sunscreen for an army.

items.text: Mo forgot the fruit, so the crew ate nuts and cheese instead.
items.reason: A surprise, but does it break a camp rule? Nuts and cheese need no cooking.

items.text: Mo toasted marshmallows over the campfire on the first night.

encounters.frame: A letter home from school has landed in the Glowerbill's tree.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that contradicts the rest. You may need to put two facts together.
encounters.success: They leave at nine and ride for two hours, so they can't start a show at ten.

parts.tap: Dear families, Years 5 and 6 will visit the Hollowgum Science Museum next Friday.
parts.reason: This sets the scene. Now find the facts about times.

parts.tap: The bus will leave school at nine o'clock sharp, so please make sure your child isn't late.
parts.reason: This is a fact to hold on to: when the bus leaves.

parts.tap: The museum is on the far side of the island, a two-hour bus ride away.
parts.reason: This is another fact. Put it together with when the bus leaves.

parts: We will spend the whole day there and eat lunch in its picnic garden.

parts.tap: Our first activity is the robot show, which starts at ten o'clock.
After lunch, students will visit the dinosaur skeleton and the famous slime lab.
parts.reason: This fits. There is plenty of time after lunch.

parts: Please pack a lunch, a drink bottle and a hat.

parts.tap: The bus will bring everyone back to school by half past five.
parts.reason: This fits. A whole day there and two hours back gets them home late.

parts: Please return the signed permission slip by Wednesday.

parts.tap: Phones must stay at home, but students may bring a camera.
parts.reason: This fits. It's an excursion rule, and no times are involved.

parts: We can't wait to see what everyone discovers!

encounters.frame: A research boat's logbook has been pinned up at the Hollowgum marina. The Glowerbill refuses to look away.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that contradicts the rest.
encounters.success: Patch has come for eleven winters running, so her first visit can't have been three winters ago.

parts.tap: For eleven winters running, a humpback whale we call Patch has travelled up this coast, and today she appeared again, right on schedule.
parts.reason: This is a fact to hold on to: eleven winters. Test later sentences against it.

parts: She is easy to recognise, because the underside of her tail is jet black except for a white splodge shaped like a lightning bolt.

parts.tap: What makes Patch remarkable is that she always migrates alone, and nobody on board has ever seen her travelling with another whale.
parts.reason: This is another fact to hold on to. Does any sentence put her with other whales?

parts: Most humpbacks move in small, loose groups, so a solitary traveller keeps the scientists guessing.

parts.tap: This morning she breached three times beside the boat, close enough that the spray drenched our cameraman.
parts.reason: Exciting, but it doesn't clash. She can come close and still travel alone.

parts.tap: Our cameraman has filmed every visit Patch has made, starting with her very first one, just three winters ago.

parts: We followed her north at a respectful distance for about four hours, recording her song through an underwater microphone.

parts.tap: Her song this year contains a new phrase, a rising whoop we have never heard from her before.
parts.reason: A surprise isn't always a clash. A new phrase can be true. Read on.

parts.tap: One theory is that she heard it from other humpbacks far away, because whale song can carry a long way underwater.
parts.reason: This fits. She can hear far-off whales without travelling with them.

parts: The captain has promised that whoever names the new phrase gets the last chocolate biscuit on board. Back on shore, we'll compare the recordings with every humpback song in our library.

encounters.frame: Zed wrote a recap of the island gaming tournament. The Glowerbill's feathers are bristling.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that contradicts the rest.
encounters.success: Darwin is outside the hall, and nobody outside could watch. So her cousin couldn't watch it live.

parts.tap: The Hollowgum Gaming Cup almost didn't happen this year, because a storm knocked out the island's internet the night before.
parts.reason: This is a fact to hold on to: no internet. Test each later sentence against it.

parts: Twenty-four players had signed up from every school on the island.

parts.tap: Instead of cancelling, the organisers linked twenty consoles together with cables in the school hall, so every match could be played offline.
parts.reason: This fits the fact. Cables let them play without the internet.

parts.tap: It meant there was no live stream, and nobody outside the hall could watch a single match.
parts.reason: This is another fact to hold on to. Who could see the matches?

parts.tap: Parents filmed the best moments on their phones so they could upload them once the internet returned.
parts.reason: This fits. They filmed inside the hall and waited to upload.

parts: Between matches, Mo ran a snack stall selling lava popcorn, which most players politely avoided. In the final, a Year 5 player called Ash faced last year's champion, who had not lost a match in two years.

parts.tap: Ash's cousin in Darwin watched the final as it happened and texted her during round three.
The final went to five rounds, and Ash won with a move nobody in the hall had seen before.
parts.reason: This fits. It happened in the hall, where people could watch.

parts.tap: Two days later, once the internet was back, Ash's mum sent the video to the whole family.
parts.reason: This fits. Sending it later, once the internet was back, matches both facts.

parts: The organisers say the cables worked so well that next year's cup might be offline on purpose.

encounters.frame: Gus is reading a council report about something disgusting under the island. The Glowerbill can smell trouble.
encounters.text: Council workers have finally begun removing the giant fatberg discovered in the sewer beneath Hollowgum's main street last month. A fatberg forms when cooking fat, oil and grease are poured down sinks, where they cool, harden and mix with wet wipes that should never have been flushed. Over time, the mass grows larger and harder, until it can block a pipe completely. This one stretches for forty metres and weighs roughly as much as three elephants. Engineers say it has set as hard as concrete. Crews in full protective suits are breaking it apart with shovels and high-pressure water jets, working in short shifts because the stench of rotting fat is almost unbearable. One worker said it was like wading through the inside of a giant, cold meat pie. Within an hour, the crew had simply rinsed the whole fatberg away with an ordinary garden hose. The council expects the job to take about three weeks and to cost more than two hundred thousand dollars. A small chunk will be preserved in a glass case at the town museum as a warning to residents. Some people living nearby have complained about the smell drifting up through drains in the street. The council is asking everyone to scrape fat into the bin instead of the sink, and to flush only toilet paper.
encounters.prompt: Gus thinks one sentence breaks the report. Which sentence clashes, and with what?
encounters.success: Concrete-hard needs shovels, water jets and three weeks. A hose in an hour can't also be true.

options.text: The museum sentence, because a chunk of fatberg would rot in a glass case.
options.reason: The report never says it would rot. Test sentences against facts the report gives.

options.text: The garden hose sentence, because the fatberg has set as hard as concrete.
The garden hose sentence, because a hose would waste too much water.
options.reason: Right sentence, wrong reason. The report never mentions wasted water. Which fact does it break?

options.text: The smell sentence, because the crews are wearing full protective suits.
options.reason: Suits protect the crews, not people in the street. Both can be true.

body.proofAsk: Tap a sentence the hose sentence clashes with.

encounters.frame: Tully is reading a concert review aloud. The Glowerbill stopped her at one line.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that contradicts the rest, then choose one that fits.
encounters.success: A wave makes no sound, so she'd have to see it. A loud gasp she could hear.

parts: Last night, the pianist Elena Vasquez gave the strangest recital the Hollowgum Town Hall has ever hosted.

parts.tap: Before she began, she tied a thick black blindfold over her eyes and said she would play without seeing a single key.
parts.reason: This is a fact to hold on to. Test each sentence against it.

parts.tap: A volunteer checked the blindfold and confirmed that she could see nothing at all.
parts.reason: This fits. It backs up the blindfold fact.

parts: She opened with a gentle lullaby, then launched into a piece so fast that her hands became a blur.

parts.tap: She played for a full hour without a single wrong note that anyone could hear.
parts.reason: Amazing, but a surprise isn't a clash. Playing well doesn't need eyes.

parts.tap: Halfway through, she smiled at a child waving in the front row and waved back.
Her final piece was a thunderous march that made the chandeliers rattle.
parts.reason: This fits. Rattling chandeliers have nothing to do with seeing.

parts.tap: The blindfold stayed in place for the entire performance, and she only removed it to take her bow.
parts.reason: This is the second fact. It agrees she never saw a thing.

parts: Several people in the front row admitted they had checked for a hidden mirror, but found nothing.

parts.tap: Asked afterwards how she did it, she said she had practised in the dark every night for a year.
parts.reason: This fits. Practising in the dark matches playing without seeing.

parts: Tickets for her next recital sold out within ten minutes.

options.text: Halfway through, she winked at a child waving in the front row.
options.reason: Winking back at a wave means seeing it. What did the blindfold stop?

options.text: Halfway through, a child in the front row gasped so loudly that she smiled.
Halfway through, she noticed a child in the front row copying her hands.
options.reason: You have to see hands to notice them copying. Could she see anything?

encounters.frame: Indi brought home a gallery guide. The Glowerbill is checking which artworks could really be in the show.
encounters.text: The sculptor Mira Okoye has one strict rule: she never buys a single material. Every piece in her new exhibition, Tideline, was made from rubbish she collected on the beaches of Hollowgum Island over two years. She walks the high-tide mark every morning with a sack, picking up bottle caps, thongs, rope, broken toys and tangled fishing line. Okoye also refuses to use glue, nails or screws, so each sculpture is held together with knots of washed-up fishing line, some of them so tiny that she ties them with tweezers. Nor will she paint anything. Every colour in the exhibition is exactly as the sea left it, which is why so many of her animals are faded blues, sun-bleached pinks and the dull green of old nets. Some pieces are enormous, like a whale skeleton three metres long built from washed-up white plastic pipes. Others are tiny, like a family of ants made from scraps of coloured net. Okoye says her rules are the point of the work, because they force visitors to notice how much plastic washes up on a single island. The exhibition runs until the end of March, and entry is free. Visitors are asked not to touch, because the knots can loosen. Children can join a beach clean-up with the artist every Saturday morning.
encounters.prompt: Could each artwork be in Tideline? Match each one to the right shelf.
encounters.success: Found rubbish, fishing-line knots, sea colours. Even a bright colour fits if the sea left it that way.

items.text: A crab made of red bottle caps, still as bright as the day they washed up, knotted with fishing line.
items.reason: Bright, but were the caps bought or painted? A surprise isn't always a clash.

items.text: A parrot made from thongs, its feathers coloured in with felt-tip pens.
items.reason: Check her rule about colour. Is every colour as the sea left it?

items.text: A turtle made from beach toys, screwed together so it won't fall apart.
items.reason: Check how she holds her pieces together. What does she refuse to use?

items.text: A family of tiny fish made from scraps of net, tied with tweezers.
items.reason: Check the material, the joins and the colour against her rules.

items.text: A pelican made from shiny new rope that she picked out at a hardware shop.
items.reason: Where does every material come from? Check her one strict rule.

encounters.frame: Zed wrote about the robot challenge. The Glowerbill thinks one sentence doesn't add up.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that contradicts the rest. Check the times carefully.
encounters.success: Trundle's whole run took eighty-eight seconds, so four cones can't have taken two minutes.

parts.tap: Our team spent six weeks building Trundle, a robot about the size of a shoebox, for the Hollowgum Robot Challenge.
parts.reason: This sets the scene. Now find the rules and the times.

parts.tap: The rules are strict: every robot must drive itself, and each one gets exactly ninety seconds to finish the course.
parts.reason: This is a fact to hold on to: ninety seconds. Test the times against it.

parts: That meant we had to program every turn in advance, using sensors that let Trundle spot the cones. The course was a twisting loop of ten orange cones laid out on a long table.

parts.tap: When the buzzer sounded, Trundle rolled forward and took two whole minutes to swerve around the first four cones.
Then a sensor got covered in dust, and Trundle started spinning in slow circles.
parts.reason: Bad luck, but it doesn't clash. Spinning can still fit inside ninety seconds.

parts: We could only watch from behind the line, groaning, as the clock ticked down.

parts.tap: Somehow, the dust shifted, and Trundle finished the course with just two seconds to spare.
parts.reason: This agrees with the ninety-second rule. Which time breaks it?

parts.tap: The scoreboard showed Trundle's time: eighty-eight seconds.
parts.reason: This agrees with finishing two seconds early. Find the time that can't fit.

parts.tap: Other robots had problems too: one drove straight off the table, and another tried to climb a judge's leg.
parts.reason: Funny, but it's about other robots. Nothing here clashes.

parts: Next year, we're building Trundle a tiny windscreen wiper.
